claim: The A1 insert of NLGN1 and NLGN3 forms a positively charged surface, with 9 of the 20 amino acids being arginine or lysine.
source: The A1 insert of NLGN1 and NLGN3 forms a positively charged surface, with 9 of the 20 amino acids being arginine or lysine (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1A-C showing the amino acid composition and structural representation of the A1 insert.

claim: The two internal cysteine residues in the A1 insert form a disulfide bond.
source: The two internal cysteine residues form a disulfide bond (Hoffman et al., 2004), contributing to the extended surface.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hoffman et al., 2004.

claim: A constitutive positively charged surface on NLGNs near the dimer interface binds the HS chain of NRXN.
source: Another constitutive positively charged surface on NLGNs near the dimer interface binds the HS chain of NRXN, an interaction that is necessary along with protein-protein interactions for full NLGN-NRXN complex formation and function (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: NLGN1 variants containing the A1 insert required higher concentrations of salt than variants lacking A1 for elution from heparin.
source: Indeed, NLGN1 variants containing the A1 insert required higher concentrations of salt than variants lacking A1 for elution from heparin (Figure 1D; all NLGN1 variants expressed in this study contain the B insert).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D demonstrating differential elution profiles from a heparin column.

claim: A1 insertion increases the affinity of NLGN1 for HS.
source: This indicates that A1 insertion increases the affinity of NLGN1 for HS.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the heparin binding assay data showing differential elution patterns.

claim: There was only a small shift in the peak of elution between NLGN1 +A1 and NLGN1 +A1A2.
source: We further wondered whether the A2 insert with its high acidic composition might counteract the effect of A1 but we observed only a small shift in the peak of elution between NLGN1 +A1 and NLGN1 +A1A2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations from the heparin binding assay.

claim: NLGN1 +A1 and +A1A2 splice forms recruited more native neuronal NRXN to contact sites than NLGN1 -A or +A2.
source: Indeed, we found that Myc-tagged NLGN1 +A1 and +A1A2 splice forms expressed on COS7 cells cocultured with rat hippocampal neurons recruited more native neuronal NRXN to contact sites than NLGN1 -A or +A2 (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from coculture assays shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Recombinant NRXN produced in HEK293 cells is poorly HS modified.
source: We used this cell-based assay to assess NRXN-NLGN1 interaction because recombinant NRXN produced in HEK293 cells is poorly HS modified (Zhang et al., 2018), making it difficult to do direct binding assays with appropriately glycosylated NRXN.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: One study using bacterially expressed NRXN1β reported a positive effect of the A1 insert on binding affinity.
source: One of these studies using bacterially expressed NRXN1β reported a positive effect of the A1 insert (Comoletti et al., 2006) although two studies using NRXN1β expressed in mammalian cells reported no difference in affinity between NLGN1 -A and NLGN1 +A1 (Elegheert et al., 2017; Koehnke et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Two studies using NRXN1β expressed in mammalian cells reported no difference in affinity between NLGN1 -A and NLGN1 +A1.
source: One of these studies using bacterially expressed NRXN1β reported a positive effect of the A1 insert (Comoletti et al., 2006) although two studies using NRXN1β expressed in mammalian cells reported no difference in affinity between NLGN1 -A and NLGN1 +A1 (Elegheert et al., 2017; Koehnke et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Elegheert et al., 2017 and Koehnke et al., 2010.

claim: The NLGN1 A1 insert does not affect binding to the NRXN LNS domain but increases binding to the NRXN HS modification.
source: Altogether, these previous results and our data suggest that the NLGN1 A1 insert does not affect binding to the NRXN LNS domain but increases binding to the NRXN HS modification.
evidence: The claim is inferred from a combination of previous studies and the current experimental data.

claim: NLGN1 A1 inserts were most prevalent in GABAergic cell types in mouse primary visual cortex, including the VIP and parvalbumin classes.
source: In mouse primary visual cortex, NLGN1 A1 inserts were most prevalent in GABAergic cell types, including the well-studied VIP and parvalbumin classes (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Oligodendrocytes showed high A1 inclusion whereas A1 was essentially absent from NLGN1 in astrocytes and oligodendrocyte precursor cells.
source: Oligodendrocytes also showed high A1 inclusion whereas A1 was essentially absent from NLGN1 in astrocytes and oligodendrocyte precursor cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: Cell type specific splicing patterns were generally similar in anterior lateral motor cortex except the Meis2-expressing divergent GABAergic neuron class showed more NLGN1 A1 inclusion.
source: Cell type specific splicing patterns were generally similar in anterior lateral motor cortex (Figure 3B) except here the Meis2-expressing divergent GABAergic neuron class showed more NLGN1 A1 inclusion.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: NLGN1 A1 inclusion was highest in GABAergic neurons of the cortex, including VIP and parvalbumin classes, in ribosome-engaged transcripts from genetically defined neuron types.
source: In this dataset of actively translated transcripts (GEO GSE133291), we again found that NLGN1 A1 inclusion was highest in GABAergic neurons of the cortex, including VIP and parvalbumin classes (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of ribosome-engaged transcript data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: NLGN1 A1 inclusion in mouse cortex peaked during the first to second postnatal weeks.
source: Developmentally, NLGN1 A1 inclusion in mouse cortex peaked during the first to second postnatal weeks (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by developmental RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Rbfox triple KO effectively eliminated NLGN1 A1 inclusion at both stages of neuron maturation.
source: Our analyses of this dataset revealed that Rbfox triple KO effectively eliminated NLGN1 A1 inclusion at both stages of neuron maturation (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data from Rbfox triple KO neurons shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Analysis of Mbnl knockout datasets essentially rules out a role for Mbnl in NLGN1 A site splicing.
source: Our analyses of these datasets essentially rules out a role for Mbnl in NLGN1 A site splicing (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data from Mbnl knockout mice shown in Figure 4D.

claim: NLGN1 A1 inclusion was reduced in the Ptbp2 Nestin-Cre KO dataset but not in the Emx1-Cre KO dataset.
source: For Ptbp2, the Emx1-Cre KO datasets did not show any difference in NLGN1 A1 splicing, but NLGN1 A1 inclusion was reduced in the Nestin-Cre KO dataset (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data from Ptbp2 knockout mice shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Ptbp2 may regulate NLGN1 -A1 splicing in neurons outside the forebrain.
source: These findings suggest Ptbp2 may regulate NLGN1 -A1 splicing in neurons outside the forebrain.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential effects observed in Nestin-Cre vs Emx1-Cre Ptbp2 knockout datasets.

claim: Transcriptomic analyses indicated a major role for Rbfox and lesser roles, if any, for Mbnl or Ptbp2 in NLGN1 A1 splicing.
source: Therefore, our transcriptomic analyses indicated a major role for Rbfox and lesser roles, if any, for Mbnl or Ptbp2 in NLGN1 A1 splicing.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined analysis of multiple RNA-seq datasets from knockout mice.

claim: NLGN1 +A1 and +A1A2 induced greater presynaptic differentiation than other splice variants in coculture assays.
source: Here we found that NLGN1 +A1 and +A1A2 induced greater presynaptic differentiation than other splice variants, assessed by synapsin clustering at axon - COS7 cell contact sites lacking dendrite contact to exclude native synapses (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from coculture assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: NLGN binding to axonal NRXN is required for synaptogenic activity in coculture, based on loss of activity upon NRXN triple knockdown or by NLGN point mutations.
source: NLGN binding to axonal NRXN is required for this synaptogenic activity in coculture, based on loss of activity upon NRXN triple knockdown (Gokce and Südhof, 2013; Zhang et al., 2018) or by NLGN point mutations that disrupt binding to the NRXN LNS domain (Ko et al., 2009) or to the NRXN HS modification (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NLGN1* +A1 induced greater presynaptic differentiation than NLGN1* -A, assessed by total intensity of VGlut1 clustering onto expressing neurons.
source: We found that NLGN1* +A1 induced greater presynaptic differentiation than NLGN1* -A, assessed by total intensity of vesicular glutamate transport VGlut1 clustering onto expressing neurons (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from molecular replacement assays shown in Figure 6A-D.

claim: There was no difference between the NLGN1 isoforms in the density of VGlut1 clusters per dendrite area.
source: There was no difference between the NLGN1 isoforms in the density of VGlut1 clusters per dendrite area, suggesting no difference in synapse numbers, but a difference in total intensity of VGlut1 per cluster.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from VGlut1 clustering assays.

claim: There was no difference in the degree of synaptic enrichment of AP-NLGN1* -A versus +A1.
source: However, there was no difference in the degree of synaptic enrichment of AP-NLGN1* -A versus +A1, nor in Homer1c-dsRed synaptic enrichment, cluster density, or cluster area between groups (Figure 6E–I).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from synaptic enrichment assays shown in Figure 6E-I.

claim: The NLGN1 A1 splice insert mediates differential recruitment of NRXN and presynaptic differentiation but not differential postsynaptic targeting.
source: Collectively, our data indicate that the NLGN1 A1 splice insert mediates differential recruitment of NRXN and presynaptic differentiation but not differential postsynaptic targeting.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data on NRXN recruitment, presynaptic differentiation, and postsynaptic localization.

claim: Neurons expressing shNlgn1 and rescued with NLGN1* +A1 had significantly greater mEPSC frequency than those rescued with NLGN1* -A.
source: Neurons expressing shNlgn1 and rescued with NLGN1* +A1 had significantly greater mEPSC frequency than those rescued with NLGN1* -A, with a corresponding reduction in mEPSC interevent interval (Figure 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 7.

claim: There was no difference between groups in mEPSC amplitude.
source: There was no difference between groups in mEPSC amplitude.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiology data.

claim: The NLGN1 A1 splice insert enhances functional transmission as well as structural presynaptic differentiation.
source: Thus, the NLGN1 A1 splice insert enhances functional transmission as well as structural presynaptic differentiation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined electrophysiology and structural data.

claim: The NLGN1 P89L missense variant was found in two ASD siblings but not in controls.
source: To test this idea, we chose the NLGN1 P89L missense variant found in two ASD siblings but not in controls (Nakanishi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nakanishi et al., 2017.

claim: Modelling in Nlgn1 P89L heterozygous knock-in mice resulted in reduced NLGN1 protein levels and deficits in social interaction, altered social dominance, and impaired spatial memory.
source: Modelling in Nlgn1 P89L heterozygous knock-in mice resulted in reduced NLGN1 protein levels and deficits in social interaction, altered social dominance, and impaired spatial memory, supporting a causative role of this mutation in autism (Nakanishi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nakanishi et al., 2017.

claim: There was a reduction in surface expression of Myc-NLGN1 -A P89L relative to WT.
source: We confirmed an expected reduction in surface expression of Myc-NLGN1 -A P89L relative to WT (Figure 8—figure supplement 1), likely reflecting enhanced endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (Nakanishi et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and a citation to Nakanishi et al., 2017.

claim: The P89L mutation significantly reduced presynaptic differentiation by NLGN1 even when cells with equal NLGN1 surface expression were chosen.
source: Interestingly, even though cells with equal NLGN1 surface expression were chosen for the coculture assay, the P89L mutation significantly reduced presynaptic differentiation by NLGN1 (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from coculture assays shown in Figure 8.

claim: NLGN1 P89L -A induced <20% of the level of synapsin clustering as wild type NLGN1 -A.
source: NLGN1 P89L -A induced <20% of the level of synapsin clustering as wild type NLGN1 -A, even after controlling for any difference in surface expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from coculture assays.

claim: The P89L mutation not only reduces total and surface levels of NLGN1 but also renders the NLGN1 that reaches the cell surface less effective at inducing presynaptic differentiation.
source: Thus, the P89L mutation not only reduces total and surface levels of NLGN1 (Nakanishi et al., 2017; Figure 8—figure supplement 1) but also renders the NLGN1 that reaches the cell surface less effective at inducing presynaptic differentiation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data on surface expression and synaptogenic activity.

claim: Addition of the A1 insert partially alleviated the deficit in presynaptic differentiation caused by the P89L mutation.
source: Importantly, addition of the A1 insert partially alleviated this deficit: NLGN1 P89L +A1 induced greater presynaptic differentiation than NLGN1 P89L -A (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from coculture assays shown in Figure 8.

claim: The total fluorescence intensity of VGlut1 inputs was higher onto hippocampal neurons expressing NLGN1* P89L +A1 than NLGN1* P89L -A.
source: Furthermore, in the native synapse molecular replacement assay with NLGN1 knockdown, the total fluorescence intensity of VGlut1 inputs was higher onto hippocampal neurons expressing NLGN1* P89L +A1 than NLGN1* P89L -A (Figure 9).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from molecular replacement assays shown in Figure 9.

claim: The A1 insert functions in the context of the P89L ASD mutation to enhance presynaptic differentiation.
source: Thus, the A1 insert functions in the context of the P89L ASD mutation to enhance presynaptic differentiation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing rescue of P89L function by A1 insertion.

claim: The A1 insert appears highly conserved among vertebrates, including humans, mice, zebrafish, and chickens.
source: Yet the A1 insert appears highly conserved among vertebrates, including humans, mice, zebrafish, and chickens (Figure 1A; Rissone et al., 2010; Wahlin et al., 2010), suggesting a functional importance.
evidence: The claim is supported by data in Figure 1A and citations to Rissone et al., 2010 and Wahlin et al., 2010.

claim: The A1 insert increases binding of NLGN1 to heparin and increases recruitment of the axonal binding partner of NLGN1, HS-modified NRXN.
source: We show here that the A1 insert increases binding of NLGN1 to heparin and increases recruitment of the axonal binding partner of NLGN1, HS-modified NRXN.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from heparin binding and coculture assays.

claim: NLGN1 A1 inclusion increases presynaptic differentiation and synaptic transmission but does not affect NLGN1 synaptic targeting or synapse density.
source: Functionally, NLGN1 A1 inclusion increases presynaptic differentiation and synaptic transmission but does not affect NLGN1 synaptic targeting or synapse density.
evidence: The claim is supported by combined experimental data from structural and functional assays.

claim: Data from KO neurons reveals regulation of A1 splicing by the Rbfox family of splicing factors.
source: Data from KO neurons reveals regulation of A1 splicing by the Rbfox family of splicing factors, and transcriptomic analyses reveals high A1 inclusion in multiple cortical GABAergic cell types.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of RNA-seq data from Rbfox knockout neurons.

claim: Transcriptomic analyses reveals high A1 inclusion in multiple cortical GABAergic cell types.
source: Data from KO neurons reveals regulation of A1 splicing by the Rbfox family of splicing factors, and transcriptomic analyses reveals high A1 inclusion in multiple cortical GABAergic cell types.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: A1 inclusion enhances function not just of wild type NLGN1 but also of the ASD-linked NLGN1 P89L mutant.
source: Finally, we show that A1 inclusion enhances function not just of wild type NLGN1 but also of the ASD-linked NLGN1 P89L mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from assays with the P89L mutant.

claim: The A splice site might be harnessed as a means to restore function in disorders involving deleterious mutations in NLGN1, and potentially NLGN3.
source: We suggest that the A splice site might be harnessed as a means to restore function in disorders involving deleterious mutations in NLGN1, and potentially NLGN3, by developing therapeutics to convert the more prevalent -A form to the more synaptogenic +A1 form.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential therapeutic application based on the experimental findings.

claim: The role identified for the NLGN1 splice site A1 insert is an unusual one, increasing NLGN1 interaction with HS glycan and thus enhancing synaptogenic function.
source: The role identified here for the NLGN1 splice site A1 insert is an unusual one, increasing NLGN1 interaction with HS glycan and thus enhancing synaptogenic function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data and comparison to other known mechanisms.

claim: A mechanism involving altered protein-glycan interaction is less common than alternative splicing regulating synapse development through altered protein-protein interactions.
source: Although there are many cases of alternative splicing regulating synapse development through altered protein-protein interactions, a mechanism involving altered protein-glycan interaction is less common.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about splicing mechanisms.

claim: The NLGN1 B splice site regulates synaptogenic function partially through N-glycosylation of the NLGN1 B insert blocking binding to α-NRXN while retaining binding to β-NRXN.
source: The NLGN1 B splice site also regulates synaptogenic function partially through glycosylation, in that case through N-glycosylation of the NLGN1 B insert blocking binding to α-NRXN while retaining binding to β-NRXN (Boucard et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Boucard et al., 2005.

claim: Neural-specific alternative splicing of agrin at its y site regulates its interaction with HS, and HS binding reduces agrin interaction with dystroglycan.
source: Neural-specific alternative splicing of agrin at its y site also regulates its interaction with HS, and HS binding reduces agrin interaction with dystroglycan (Gesemann et al., 1996; O'Toole et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gesemann et al., 1996 and O'Toole et al., 1996.

claim: The y site and these interactions are not critical for agrin synaptogenic activity.
source: However, the y site and these interactions are not critical for agrin synaptogenic activity (Burgess et al., 1999; Li et al., 2018), unlike the central role of the NRXN interaction for NLGN1 function.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Burgess et al., 1999 and Li et al., 2018.

claim: The NLGN1 A1 insert had no apparent effect on the synaptic targeting of NLGN1.
source: However, the NLGN1 A1 insert had no apparent effect on the synaptic targeting of NLGN1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from synaptic enrichment assays.

claim: The excitatory postsynaptic localization of NLGN1 is largely controlled by intracellular interactions regulated by multiple kinases.
source: This finding is consistent with other data suggesting that the excitatory postsynaptic localization of NLGN1 is largely controlled by intracellular interactions regulated by multiple kinases (Jeong et al., 2019; Jeong et al., 2017; Letellier et al., 2020; Letellier et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The NLGN1 +A1-associated increase in mEPSC frequency and VGlut1 cluster intensity without a change in VGlut1 or Homer1c-dsRed cluster density suggest there is no change in synapse numbers but rather an increase in neurotransmitter release.
source: The NLGN1 +A1-associated increase in mEPSC frequency and VGlut1 cluster intensity without a change in VGlut1 or Homer1c-dsRed cluster density suggest there is no change in synapse numbers but rather an increase in neurotransmitter release.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data on mEPSC frequency, VGlut1 intensity, and cluster density.

claim: These findings are consistent with previous reports of a retrograde effect of NLGN1 on neurotransmitter release probability.
source: These findings are consistent with previous reports of a retrograde effect of NLGN1 on neurotransmitter release probability (Futai et al., 2007; Stan et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Futai et al., 2007 and Stan et al., 2010.

claim: The lack of effect of the NLGN1 A1 insert on mEPSC amplitude suggests no effect on postsynaptic sensitivity.
source: In contrast, the lack of effect of the NLGN1 A1 insert on mEPSC amplitude suggests no effect on postsynaptic sensitivity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the electrophysiology data showing no difference in mEPSC amplitude.

claim: The data are consistent with a purely retrograde mechanism of action of the NLGN1 A1 insert through enhanced NRXN recruitment mediating enhanced presynaptic differentiation and increased transmitter release rate.
source: Thus, altogether our data are consistent with a purely retrograde mechanism of action of the NLGN1 A1 insert through enhanced NRXN recruitment mediating enhanced presynaptic differentiation and increased transmitter release rate.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental data on NRXN recruitment, presynaptic differentiation, and synaptic transmission.

claim: The A1 insert in NLGN3 regulates GABAergic transmission, as overexpression of NLGN3 +A1 or +A1A2 reduced GABAergic transmission whereas NLGN3 -A or +A2 increased GABAergic transmission relative to neighbour untransfected cells in hippocampal slice cultures.
source: While this work was under revision, it was reported that the A1 insert in NLGN3 regulates GABAergic transmission, as overexpression of NLGN3 +A1 or +A1A2 reduced GABAergic transmission whereas NLGN3 -A or +A2 increased GABAergic transmission relative to neighbour untransfected cells in hippocampal slice cultures (Uchigashima et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Uchigashima et al., 2020.

claim: The mechanism of the effect of the A1 insert in NLGN3 on GABAergic transmission may also involve differential interactions with NRXN -HS.
source: We suggest that the mechanism of this effect may also involve differential interactions with NRXN -HS.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a mechanism based on the findings with NLGN1.

claim: The effect of the higher NLGN1 A1 inclusion in GABAergic than in glutamatergic neuron classes may be to increase excitatory input selectively onto the GABAergic neurons, thus enhancing synchrony of the overall network.
source: The effect of the higher NLGN1 A1 inclusion in GABAergic than in glutamatergic neuron classes may be to increase excitatory input selectively onto the GABAergic neurons, thus enhancing synchrony of the overall network.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a functional consequence based on the cell-type specific expression pattern.

claim: Cortical VIP and parvalbumin interneurons play key roles in neural synchrony and cognitive processing.
source: In particular, cortical VIP and parvalbumin interneurons, which showed high NLGN1 A1 inclusion in all datasets, play key roles in neural synchrony and cognitive processing.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about the function of these interneuron types.

claim: VIP interneuron disinhibition of prefrontal responses to hippocampal inputs controls avoidance behaviour.
source: For example, VIP interneuron disinhibition of prefrontal responses to hippocampal inputs controls avoidance behaviour (Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2019.

claim: NLGN3 on parvalbumin interneurons contributes to gamma oscillations and social behaviour as well as fear conditioning.
source: NLGN3 on parvalbumin interneurons contributes to gamma oscillations and social behaviour as well as fear conditioning (Cao et al., 2018; Polepalli et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cao et al., 2018 and Polepalli et al., 2017.

claim: Unlike the highly dedicated splicing program of SLM2 regulating synaptic properties through NRXN site 4 splicing, the Rbfox family regulates a broader range of targets controlling synaptic properties and other aspects of neuronal maturation including axon initial segment assembly.
source: Unlike the highly dedicated splicing program of SLM2 regulating synaptic properties through NRXN site 4 splicing (Traunmüller et al., 2016), the Rbfox family regulates a broader range of targets controlling synaptic properties and other aspects of neuronal maturation including axon initial segment assembly (Jacko et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Traunmüller et al., 2016 and Jacko et al., 2018.

claim: In GABAergic neurons, a mechanism involving Rbfox1 binding to the Vamp1 mRNA 3' UTR regulates synaptic transmission.
source: Rbfox proteins also act as more than just splicing factors; in GABAergic neurons, a mechanism involving Rbfox1 binding to the Vamp1 mRNA 3' UTR regulates synaptic transmission (Vuong et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vuong et al., 2018.

claim: RBFOX1 is a risk gene for ASD based on strong evidence including de novo copy number deletions.
source: Like NLGNs, RBFOX1 is a risk gene for ASD based on strong evidence including de novo copy number deletions (Sebat et al., 2007; Zhao, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sebat et al., 2007 and Zhao, 2013.

claim: Elevating A1 insertion is a promising direction to enhance the function of NLGN1 in cases of deleterious mutations.
source: The results here with the P89L NLGN1 mutant support the idea that elevating A1 insertion is a promising direction to enhance the function of NLGN1 in cases of deleterious mutations.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing partial rescue of P89L function by A1 insertion.

claim: This approach will likely extend to NLGN3 as well as NLGN1, given their high sequence homology including the A1 insert.
source: This approach will likely extend to NLGN3 as well as NLGN1, given their high sequence homology including the A1 insert (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing that the findings will extend to NLGN3 based on sequence homology.

claim: NLGN3 is among the top risk genes for ASD with multiple functionally deleterious missense mutations.
source: NLGN3 is among the top risk genes for ASD with multiple functionally deleterious missense mutations (Jamain et al., 2003; Quartier et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Jamain et al., 2003 and Quartier et al., 2019.

claim: In the majority of cases which involve heterozygous mutations, reagents that increase A1 insertion could act by enhancing function of both the mutant NLGN and the wild type allele.
source: In the majority of cases which involve heterozygous mutations, reagents that increase A1 insertion could act by enhancing function of both the mutant NLGN and the wild type allele.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a therapeutic mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: NRXN1 is among the top risk genes for ASD as well as for schizophrenia and Tourette's Syndrome.
source: NRXN1 is also among the top risk genes for ASD as well as for schizophrenia and Tourette's Syndrome (Tourette Syndrome Association International Consortium for Genetics (TSAICG) et al., 2017; Rees et al., 2014; Südhof, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Therapies targeting wild type NLGN splicing to elevate the function of NLGN-NRXN complexes may also be partially efficacious in cases of NRXN mutations.
source: Therapies targeting wild type NLGN splicing to elevate the function of NLGN-NRXN complexes may also be partially efficacious in cases of NRXN mutations.
evidence: The claim is speculative, proposing a potential therapeutic application.

claim: Clinically effective oligonucleotide reagents targeting splicing events have reached the bedside for other disorders, notably for increasing specific exon inclusion in SMN2 to treat spinal muscular atrophy.
source: Clinically effective oligonucleotide reagents targeting splicing events have reached the bedside for other disorders, notably for increasing specific exon inclusion in SMN2 to treat spinal muscular atrophy (Bennett et al., 2019; Singh et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bennett et al., 2019 and Singh et al., 2017.

claim: NLGNs bind to two interfaces on NRXN, to the laminin-neurexin-sex hormone (LNS) protein domain and to the heparan sulphate (HS) glycan chain.
source: NLGNs bind to two interfaces on NRXN, to the laminin-neurexin-sex hormone (LNS) protein domain and to the heparan sulphate (HS) glycan chain (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: Mutations in all NLGN and NRXN genes are associated with neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: Mutations in all NLGN and NRXN genes are associated with neuropsychiatric disorders.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about NLGN and NRXN genes.

claim: NLGNs and NRXNs are evolutionarily conserved and essential for mouse survival.
source: NLGNs and NRXNs are evolutionarily conserved and essential for mouse survival (Missler et al., 2003; Varoqueaux et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Missler et al., 2003 and Varoqueaux et al., 2006.

claim: MDGA binding to NLGNs occludes the NRXN binding site, thus preventing NLGN-NRXN interaction and suppressing synapse development.
source: MDGA binding to NLGNs occludes the NRXN binding site, thus preventing NLGN-NRXN interaction and suppressing synapse development.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about MDGA-NLGN interactions.

claim: NLGNs can bind to the excitatory postsynaptic scaffold PSD-95 and the inhibitory postsynaptic scaffold gephyrin, interactions that are regulated by phosphorylation.
source: Intracellularly, NLGNs can bind to the excitatory postsynaptic scaffold PSD-95 and the inhibitory postsynaptic scaffold gephyrin, interactions that are regulated by phosphorylation (Jeong et al., 2019; Jeong et al., 2017; Letellier et al., 2020; Letellier et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: NLGN1 functions at excitatory glutamatergic synapses, NLGN2 at inhibitory GABAergic synapses, and NLGN3 at both.
source: NLGN1 functions at excitatory glutamatergic synapses, NLGN2 at inhibitory GABAergic synapses, and NLGN3 at both.
evidence: The claim draws from established scientific knowledge about NLGN function.

claim: NLGN1 is essential for normal NMDA receptor recruitment, long-term potentiation, and spatial learning and memory.
source: NLGN1 is essential for normal NMDA receptor recruitment, long-term potentiation, and spatial learning and memory (Blundell et al., 2010; Budreck et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2017; Shipman and Nicoll, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Additional competitive effects of NLGN1 on synapse number were revealed with sparse knockdown.
source: Additional competitive effects of NLGN1 on synapse number were revealed with sparse knockdown (Kwon et al., 2012) and roles in long-term depression revealed in Nlgn1 heterozygous mice (Dang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kwon et al., 2012 and Dang et al., 2018.

claim: Copy number, truncating, and missense variants in NLGN1 are associated with autism spectrum disorders (ASD).
source: Copy number, truncating, and missense variants in NLGN1 are associated with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) (Glessner et al., 2009; Nakanishi et al., 2017; O'Roak et al., 2012; Tejada et al., 2019) and obsessive-compulsive disorder (Gazzellone et al., 2016) and NLGN1 polymorphisms are linked to schizophrenia (Chen et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The A1 insert increases the binding of NLGN1 to HS, a modification on NRXN, increasing NLGN1 synaptogenic activity.
source: Here, we show that the A1 insert increases the binding of NLGN1 to HS, a modification on NRXN, increasing NLGN1 synaptogenic activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from heparin binding and synaptogenic assays.

claim: A1 insertion can partially restore function of an ASD-linked missense variant of NLGN1.
source: We further report cell type regulation of A1 insertion, identify Rbfox1-3 as potential regulators, and show that A1 insertion can partially restore function of an ASD-linked missense variant of NLGN1.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from assays with the P89L mutant.
